text: Northbridge Retail's checkout and product-catalog services already run in Docker containers. That part's done. The problem is everything around the containers — which machine runs which container, what happens when one crashes, how you scale for Black Friday. That's what this lesson, and this course, is about.

Past a handful of containers, new problems show up. With services spread across fifteen VMs, something has to decide which host has room for the next container. When one crashes at two in the morning, something has to notice and restart it. And when Black Friday needs ten times the normal checkout capacity for six hours, a shell script SSHing into servers doesn't hold up.

None of that is a Docker problem — Docker runs one container correctly, full stop. Kubernetes is a container orchestrator: you tell it the end state you want, like "three replicas of checkout-service, always," and it continuously works to keep reality matching that promise, restarting and rescheduling containers whenever something drifts.

That's the declarative model. An imperative script runs a command once and moves on — it has no idea if the container dies five minutes later. Kubernetes keeps comparing desired state to actual state, forever, and closes the gap automatically. Docker still builds and runs the individual container; Kubernetes decides where, how many, and reacts when something changes.

Northbridge's existing container images don't change at all to run on Kubernetes — what changes is the placement, scaling, healing, and networking around them. Next up, lesson two: the control plane and nodes that actually run this reconciliation loop.
